lead: Travel changes the viewpoint through a virtual world. Wayfinding is the user's plan for where to go and how to stay oriented. The two work together: a fast travel method is useless if the user cannot decide the next turn. Virtual campuses, VR training rooms and AR walking guides all need both. Some syllabi call the whole topic navigation; this chapter keeps travel, the movement, separate from wayfinding, the knowledge and aids that guide movement.
prereq: You need Chapter 5.1 for manipulation versus travel, and Unit 2 for trackers that measure head and hand motion.

blocks.text: Travel is the control of the viewpoint. The user moves through the scene, while objects stay fixed. A travel technique has a selection method (where to go) and a motion method (how to get there). Three travel tasks cover most exercises. Exploration has no fixed target; the user learns the layout. Search has a target, such as a fire exit. Manoeuvring is small, precise motion, such as lining up with a door handle.

items: Physical walking maps real steps to virtual motion. It feels natural but needs tracked floor space.
Steering gives continuous control through a joystick, hand direction or gaze. It is like driving.
Fly adds vertical control. It suits open 3D scenes but can cause discomfort.
Gaze-directed travel moves where the head or eyes point. Hands stay free, but small gaze shifts cause drift.
Point-and-go selects a far point and then moves the user there. It reduces continuous input.
Teleport jumps to a marked place. It is fast and reduces motion sickness, but it weakens the sense of continuous space.
World scaling changes the apparent size of the world or the user, so a small tracked area can cover a large virtual campus.

blocks.text: Choose by task. Use teleport or point-and-go for long searches; use physical walking or slow steering for precise manoeuvring. The worked example below uses a simple map, not a headset, to show route length versus straight-line distance.

Wayfinding is the cognitive side of navigation. The user decides a route, keeps orientation and recognises the destination. Three ideas from spatial cognition help. A landmark is a salient object used as a reference. Route knowledge is a sequence of turns along a path. Survey knowledge is a map-like view of the whole area. Users often learn route knowledge first and survey knowledge later, so a virtual world should support both.

items: Maps and minimaps show position; a north-up map is stable, a forward-up map matches the view.
Signs and labels at decision points give the next action, such as 'Exit B, 20 m'.
Guides, arrows, audio cues or a virtual agent point the way; they must be removable.
Layout with clear paths, open sightlines and short decision points reduces wrong turns.
Lighting makes exits, stairs and landmarks visible without glare.
Distinct landmarks and district colours at junctions help users build survey knowledge.

blocks.text: Evaluate aids by time to target, wrong turns, map checks, layout recall and confidence. Test new users, not only the design team. A minimap may shorten perceived effort while the physical path stays the same. Keep signs consistent, show 'you are here', do not rely on colour alone, and allow aids to be switched off.

Match the travel method to the wayfinding aid. A large campus with many destinations suits teleport plus a minimap and repeated landmarks. A training bench suits physical walking or slow steering, because small hand and body motions matter. A search task suits point-and-go plus a sign at the target. Reduce discomfort by using snap turns, teleport or limited acceleration, and see Chapter 5.7 for health checks. Keep one aid per decision point. Too many arrows hide the landmarks that users need for survey knowledge. The worked example compares the walked route with the straight-line distance; the dashed edge in the figure is that shorter distance.

Design the world and the interface together. If the map shows a shortcut, the world must allow it. If a sign says 'East Wing', the east wing must be visible from that point. Test the aid with a new user who has not seen the map. Ask the user to point to the start after reaching the target; this checks survey knowledge, not just route following.

spec.aria: A map grid with a solid path from Start at (0, 0) east to (3, 0) and north to Final at (3, 4), and a dashed straight line of 5 m from Start to Final.

examples.question: A virtual campus has the user at (0, 0) m on a map. The user walks 3 m east, then 4 m north. Compute the straight-line distance from start to final point and compare it with the route length.
steps: Start S = (0, 0) m. After walking east, E = (3, 0) m. After walking north, F = (3, 4) m.
Horizontal change Δx = 3 − 0 = 3 m. Vertical change Δy = 4 − 0 = 4 m.
Straight-line distance d = √(Δx² + Δy²) = √(3² + 4²) m = √(9 + 16) m = √25 m = 5 m.
Route is longer by 7 − 5 = 2 m. Route divided by straight-line distance is 7 ÷ 5 = 1.4.
examples.answer: The straight-line distance is 5 m; the walked route is 7 m, which is 2 m longer.
examples.check:
import math
x0, y0 = 0.0, 0.0
x1, y1 = 3.0, 0.0
x2, y2 = 3.0, 4.0
route = math.hypot(x1 - x0, y1 - y0) + math.hypot(x2 - x1, y2 - y1)
straight = math.hypot(x2 - x0, y2 - y0)
print(straight)
print(route)
print(route - straight)
print(route / straight)

traps: Route length is not straight-line distance. A 3 m + 4 m walk has route 7 m but straight-line 5 m.
Travel is movement; wayfinding is the decision of where to move. A map does not move the user.
Physical walking is natural but limited by tracked space; teleport covers large distances but can break continuous spatial knowledge.
User-centred aids are added to the interface (map, sign, guide). Environment-centred aids are built into the world (layout, lighting, landmarks).
Gaze-directed travel uses head or eye direction continuously; point-and-go selects a target and then moves. Do not swap them.

quiz.q: Define travel in a VR system.
quiz.a: Travel is the technique that changes the user's viewpoint and moves the user through the virtual world.
Any two of: minimap, sign, arrow guide, audio cue, virtual guide.

quiz.q: Distinguish route knowledge from survey knowledge.
quiz.a: Route knowledge is a sequence of turns along a path. Survey knowledge is a map-like overview of the whole area and the relations between places.

quiz.q: Why can teleport reduce motion sickness compared with continuous fly?
quiz.a: Teleport removes continuous optic flow during travel, so there is less conflict with the vestibular sense. Sudden jumps can still reduce spatial continuity.

quiz.q: A user walks 6 m east and 8 m north. Find the route length and the straight-line distance.
quiz.a: Route length = 6 + 8 = 14 m. Straight-line distance = √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10 m.

quiz.q: A minimap reduces search time but users still walk the same route. Which measure changed and which did not?
quiz.a: Search time changed; physical route length did not. Perceived effort may also change, but that is a separate subjective measure.

quiz.q: Choose one travel technique for precise manoeuvring near a door and one for crossing a large campus. Justify both.
quiz.a: Precise manoeuvring: physical walking or slow steering, because small controlled motions matter. Large campus: teleport or point-and-go, because distance is large and continuous motion may cause discomfort.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry VR uses redirected walking, where the tracked physical path is bent slightly so the user walks a virtual straight line in a small room. AR wayfinding overlays arrows on the camera view, and researchers test whether those arrows help or distract. Search terms: redirected walking, spatial cognition in VR, wayfinding aids in AR, teleportation and presence.
